Next 7 Days...

The first system of the week is beginning to make its presence
known as it continues to advect in cloud cover from the SW. Over
the next few hours the first rain/snow showers will move into
south-central MT. All of this is being forced by a negatively
tilted shortwave moving out of the Great Basin and through the
Snake River Plain. As the region of greatest diffluence and CVA
moves over the WY mountains, lee cyclogenesis is forecast to 
occur. As the surface low develops overnight, the upper level 
flow will quickly kick it to the northeast moving over southeast 
MT early Wednesday and into the Dakotas by the afternoon. 

Rainfall totals with this event have trended up slightly over the
past day or so with nearly everyone west of a KSHR to KBHK line 
forecast to see at least 0.1" of liquid. Totals up to 0.25" cannot
be ruled out, with the greatest chance just to the southeast of 
Billings. All mountains across the CWA will receive between 
0.25-0.5" SWE with some locations, esepcailly in the Bighorns, 
potentially getting up to 0.75". Even with this much liquid, snow 
ratios will start off close to 10:1 which will keep totals below 
warning criteria. The winter weather advisory in the foothills 
near Livingston and Judith Gap remains in effect due to the 
combination of snow with periods of blowing snow. The greatest 
risk for blowing snow wil be near Judith Gap due to the favorable 
wind direction. The impacts may be limited by the low SLRs and 
mismatch in wind/snow timing though. For the Livingston area, 
widespread 1" is forecast with locations in the Paradise Valley 
likely to see 2" or more. Higher elevations will pick up notably 
more snowfall due to the quick p-type changeover as well as higher
SLRs. The peak of the Bozeman Pass could accumulate up to 6" 
throughout the event.

The other story with this system will be the strong winds. Much of
the CWA will see gusts in excess of 40 mph Wednesday afternoon as
the surface low moves NE and deepens. The US-191 corridor gap 
winds may briefly reach into the 50s mph but this will be short 
lived as the tightest pressure gradient quickly moves out over 
the plains. Speaking of the plains, this is where the strongest 
winds will be. Baker, MT will see some of the strongest gusts in 
the CWA as the center of the low passes nearby while it continues
to deepen. Frequent gusts in the 50s mph with occasional 60s mph 
are forecast Wednesday afternoon. Although winds will be strong 
farther to the west, they do not quite meet warning criteria. 
Regardless of a headline or not, all locations in the forecast 
area will see strong winds Wednesday. It is also worth keeping an 
eye on the mountain wave potential Wednesday and Thursday AM over 
the Bighorns and near Sheridan as there is a signal that some 
strong winds could make their way into populated areas. If this 
were to occur it should be brief. Each morning all the ingredients
will only be aligned for a short period of time before conditions
quickly change. 

As the midweek system moves out of the area, some weak ridging
will build in Thursday. While this will not do much to rebound
temperatures, it will briefly dry out the region before the next
round of precip. Thursday and Friday mornings could come with 
areas of fog though as clear skies and calm winds will promote fog
development in conjunction with the increased surface moisture
left behind from the recent precip.

The system forecast to impact the area late week into the weekend
still has many questions surrounding it. The GFS and ECMWF, as 
well as their ensembles, have come into agreement now that the 
trough moving in off of the Pacific will be shoved a bit to the 
south as a small upper low dives down the front range of the 
Canadian Rockies. This will keep a majority of the energy and 
moisture from this system out of our forecast area, thus bringing
snow totals down. The NBM and ECMWF ensemble both show a good 
chance that much of the region will see some accumulating snow, 
it just appears that it will be less than 1". The latest 
deterministic NBM and long range models are showing 1-2" above 
4kft and up to 6" in the mountains. This event could still be a
good novelty first snow for the region, but impacts outside of 
recreation are looking increasingly less likely. WMR
